744	// recordSupersedes is project.Memory's rule, which is the one every projection
745	// owes the others. Class first, then the class's own rule.
746	func recordSupersedes(heldClass record.Class, held record.Value, nextClass record.Class, next record.Value) bool {
747		if heldClass != nextClass {
748			return nextClass > heldClass
749		}
750		return record.Supersedes(nextClass, held, next)
751	}

753	// Delete records that a value was unbound. A tombstone is a row carrying a
754	// stamp and nothing else, because a later write has to be able to beat it.
755	func (s *recordSink) Delete(k record.Key, field string, v record.Value) error {
756		return s.Put(k, record.ClassMutable, field, record.Value{Stamp: v.Stamp, Deleted: true})
757	}

759	// SetDeleteFloor need not flush: a floor is its own table, and hides fields by
760	// comparison at read time rather than by touching them.
761	func (s *recordSink) SetDeleteFloor(k record.Key, floor stamp.Stamp) error {
762		_, err := s.tx.Exec(s.ctx,
763			`INSERT INTO repo_record_floors (repo_id, schema_name, type, id, lamport, writer, seq, tick)
764			 VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7, $8)
765			 ON CONFLICT (repo_id, schema_name, type, id) DO UPDATE SET
766			     lamport = EXCLUDED.lamport, writer = EXCLUDED.writer, seq = EXCLUDED.seq, tick = EXCLUDED.tick
767			 WHERE (EXCLUDED.lamport, EXCLUDED.writer, EXCLUDED.seq)
768			     > (repo_record_floors.lamport, repo_record_floors.writer, repo_record_floors.seq)`,
769			s.p.repoID, s.p.schemaName, k.Type, k.ID, int64(floor.L), floor.Writer, int64(floor.Seq), s.tick)
770		return err
771	}
772	
773	// Expire drops a type's facts decided below a Lamport value.
774	//
775	// Facts only, and by whole record: a fact binds to record.WholeRecord, so the
776	// row deciding whether a record expired is that field's. A cutoff rather than a
777	// list of what went, which is what lets it be re-applied.
778	func (s *recordSink) Expire(typ string, below uint64) error {
779		if err := s.flush(); err != nil {
780			return err
781		}
782		_, err := s.tx.Exec(s.ctx,
783			`DELETE FROM repo_record_fields
784			 WHERE repo_id = $1 AND schema_name = $2 AND type = $3 AND id IN (
785			     SELECT id FROM repo_record_fields
786			     WHERE repo_id = $1 AND schema_name = $2 AND type = $3
787			       AND field = '' AND class = $4 AND lamport < $5)`,
788			s.p.repoID, s.p.schemaName, typ, int16(record.ClassFact), int64(below))
789		return err
790	}
791	
792	// Erase removes what an erasure names, where the deciding stamp is below its
793	// bound.
794	//
795	// Fields only. A delete floor is a stamp rather than content -- it says a delete
796	// happened, not what was deleted -- so project.Memory and generation.Erase keep
797	// a non-zero one with nothing beside it. Sweeping an emptied floor would unhide
798	// the record the moment an older write arrived.
799	//
800	// The bound is the one part of erasure.Covers restated here; the rest is the
801	// shape of the WHERE clause.
802	func (s *recordSink) Erase(e erasure.Erasure) error {
803		if err := s.flush(); err != nil {
804			return err
805		}
806		args := []any{s.p.repoID, s.p.schemaName, e.Type, int64(e.Below)}
807		where := `repo_id = $1 AND schema_name = $2 AND type = $3 AND lamport < $4`
808		switch e.Kind {
809		case erasure.ErasePartition:
810			// A partition names itself and everything nested under it, by its own
811			// field -- Partition, not ID, which a partition erasure leaves empty.
812			where += ` AND (id = $5 OR (id > $6 AND id < $7))`
813			args = append(args, e.Partition, e.Partition+"/", e.Partition+"0")
814		case erasure.EraseField:
815			// A field erasure never names the empty field, which is where a
816			// mirrored value and a fact live -- see erasure.Names.
817			where += ` AND id = $5 AND field = $6 AND field <> ''`
818			args = append(args, e.ID, e.Field)
819		default:
820			where += ` AND id = $5`
821			args = append(args, e.ID)
822		}
823		_, err := s.tx.Exec(s.ctx, `DELETE FROM repo_record_fields WHERE `+where, args...)
824		return err
825	}
826	
827	// Fields returns one record's visible fields, which is half of
828	// entire-records' store.Projection.
829	//
830	// Visible means bound and above the record's delete floor -- the same rule a
831	// fold applies, asked of rows instead of memory. A record exists if it has any
832	// field row at all, visible or not, which is why this reads the table and
833	// applies visibility here: a record whose fields are all hidden is one that
834	// currently shows nothing, not an absent one, and asking for only the visible
835	// ones would need a second query to tell those apart.
836	func (p *RecordProjection) Fields(typ, id string) (map[string][]byte, bool, error) {
837		rows, err := p.reader().Query(p.readCtx(),
838			`SELECT f.field, f.value, f.deleted,
839			        (fl.repo_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT (f.lamport, f.writer, f.seq) > (fl.lamport, fl.writer, fl.seq))
840			 FROM repo_record_fields f
841			 LEFT JOIN repo_record_floors fl
842			        ON fl.repo_id = f.repo_id AND fl.schema_name = f.schema_name
843			       AND fl.type = f.type AND fl.id = f.id
844			 WHERE f.repo_id = $1 AND f.schema_name = $2 AND f.type = $3 AND f.id = $4`,
845			p.repoID, p.schemaName, typ, id)
846		if err != nil {
847			return nil, false, err
848		}
849		defer rows.Close()
850		out, held := map[string][]byte{}, false
851		for rows.Next() {
852			var field string
853			var value []byte
854			var deleted, floored bool
855			if err := rows.Scan(&field, &value, &deleted, &floored); err != nil {
856				return nil, false, err
857			}
858			held = true
859			if !deleted && !floored {
860				out[field] = value
861			}
862		}
863		return out, held, rows.Err()
864	}
865	
866	// Under returns every record of one type at id or beneath it, with its visible
867	// fields.
868	//
869	// One statement, and a range rather than a scan. A nested record's id is its
870	// container's plus "/" and its own, so everything under a container sits in
871	// ["<id>/", "<id>0") -- '0' being the byte after '/'. The id column is C
872	// collation for exactly this: under a linguistic one the comparison does not
873	// mean what it means here.
874	func (p *RecordProjection) Under(typ, id string) (map[string]map[string][]byte, error) {
875		rows, err := p.reader().Query(p.readCtx(),
876			`SELECT f.id, f.field, f.value
877			 FROM repo_record_fields f
878			 LEFT JOIN repo_record_floors fl
879			        ON fl.repo_id = f.repo_id AND fl.schema_name = f.schema_name
880			       AND fl.type = f.type AND fl.id = f.id
881			 WHERE f.repo_id = $1 AND f.schema_name = $2 AND f.type = $3
882			   AND (f.id = $4 OR (f.id > $5 AND f.id < $6))
883			   AND f.deleted = false
884			   AND (fl.repo_id IS NULL OR (f.lamport, f.writer, f.seq) > (fl.lamport, fl.writer, fl.seq))`,
885			p.repoID, p.schemaName, typ, id, id+"/", id+"0")
886		if err != nil {
887			return nil, err
888		}
889		defer rows.Close()
890		out := map[string]map[string][]byte{}
891		for rows.Next() {
892			var recordID, field string
893			var value []byte
894			if err := rows.Scan(&recordID, &field, &value); err != nil {
895				return nil, err
896			}
897			at, ok := out[recordID]
898			if !ok {
899				at = map[string][]byte{}
900				out[recordID] = at
901			}
902			at[field] = value
903		}
904		return out, rows.Err()
905	}

907	// ChangedSince names every record a tick after `tick` wrote, with the rows that
908	// moved. It cannot see what an expiry or erasure removed: those delete rows, so
909	// a caller compares those sets itself.
910	func (p *RecordProjection) ChangedSince(tick uint64) ([]recordchange.Record, error) {
911		rows, err := p.reader().Query(p.readCtx(),
912			`WITH changed AS (
913			     SELECT type, id, field, value, deleted, writer FROM repo_record_fields
914			     WHERE repo_id = $1 AND schema_name = $2 AND tick > $3
915			 ), floors AS (
916			     SELECT type, id, writer FROM repo_record_floors
917			     WHERE repo_id = $1 AND schema_name = $2 AND tick > $3
918			 ), keys AS (
919			     SELECT type, id FROM changed UNION SELECT type, id FROM floors
920			 )
921			 SELECT k.type, k.id, c.field, c.value, COALESCE(c.deleted, false), COALESCE(c.writer, ''),
922			        COALESCE(rose.writer, ''),
923			        EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM repo_record_fields f
924			                LEFT JOIN repo_record_floors fl
925			                       ON fl.repo_id = f.repo_id AND fl.schema_name = f.schema_name
926			                      AND fl.type = f.type AND fl.id = f.id
927			                WHERE f.repo_id = $1 AND f.schema_name = $2 AND f.type = k.type AND f.id = k.id
928			                  AND f.tick <= $3 AND NOT f.deleted
929			                  AND (fl.repo_id IS NULL OR (f.lamport, f.writer, f.seq) > (fl.lamport, fl.writer, fl.seq)))
930			 FROM keys k
931			 LEFT JOIN changed c ON c.type = k.type AND c.id = k.id
932			 LEFT JOIN floors rose ON rose.type = k.type AND rose.id = k.id
933			 ORDER BY k.type, k.id`,
934			p.repoID, p.schemaName, int64(tick))
935		if err != nil {
936			return nil, err
937		}
938		defer rows.Close()
939		var out []recordchange.Record
940		for rows.Next() {
941			var key record.Key
942			var field *string
943			var f recordchange.Field
944			var floorWriter string
945			var held bool
946			if err := rows.Scan(&key.Type, &key.ID, &field, &f.Value, &f.Deleted, &f.Writer, &floorWriter, &held); err != nil {
947				return nil, err
948			}
949			if n := len(out); n == 0 || out[n-1].Key != key {
950				out = append(out, recordchange.Record{Key: key, FloorWriter: floorWriter, Held: held})
951			}
952			if field != nil {
953				f.Field = *field
954				out[len(out)-1].Fields = append(out[len(out)-1].Fields, f)
955			}
956		}
957		return out, rows.Err()
958	}

960	func (p *RecordProjection) reader() querier {
961		if p.q != nil {
962			return p.q
963		}
964		return p.s.pool
965	}

967	// readCtx is the context the two Projection reads run under.
968	//
969	// store.Projection takes none -- it is entire-records' interface, shaped for a
970	// fold that cannot block -- so the one a projection was built with is used.
971	// Bound at construction rather than per call, because the interface beneath
972	// has no room for one.
973	func (p *RecordProjection) readCtx() context.Context {
974		if p.ctx == nil {
975			return context.Background()
976		}
977		return p.ctx
978	}

980	// Visible answers what a reader would see at one slot, stamp included.
981	//
982	// Fields answers the decode's question, names and bytes for one record. This
983	// answers a conformance harness's: one slot at a time, plus the stamp that
984	// decided it, which a suite comparing two projections has to see.
985	func (p *RecordProjection) Visible(k record.Key, field string) (record.Value, bool, error) {
986		var v record.Value
987		var lamport, seq int64
988		var deleted bool
989		err := p.reader().QueryRow(p.readCtx(),
990			`SELECT f.value, f.version, f.deleted, f.lamport, f.writer, f.seq
991			 FROM repo_record_fields f
992			 LEFT JOIN repo_record_floors fl
993			        ON fl.repo_id = f.repo_id AND fl.schema_name = f.schema_name
994			       AND fl.type = f.type AND fl.id = f.id
995			 WHERE f.repo_id = $1 AND f.schema_name = $2 AND f.type = $3 AND f.id = $4 AND f.field = $5
996			   AND (fl.repo_id IS NULL OR (f.lamport, f.writer, f.seq) > (fl.lamport, fl.writer, fl.seq))`,
997			p.repoID, p.schemaName, k.Type, k.ID, field).
998			Scan(&v.Bytes, &v.Version, &deleted, &lamport, &v.Stamp.Writer, &seq)
999		switch {
1000		case errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows):
1001			return record.Value{}, false, nil
1002		case err != nil:
1003			// Before the deleted check, so a Scan that failed half-way cannot be
1004			// read as an answer.
1005			return record.Value{}, false, err
1006		case deleted:
1007			return record.Value{}, false, nil
1008		}
1009		v.Stamp.L, v.Stamp.Seq = uint64(lamport), uint64(seq)
1010		return v, true, nil
1011	}

1014	// route to. A conformance harness has its own; so would a backfill replaying a

1017		_, err := p.Tick(ctx, heldBatch{b})
1018		return err

# Records are read through entire-records' own decode

Status: accepted, 2026-08-10; amended 2026-10-01 (records move to the v0 surface); amended 2026-10-10 (reads come from strata)

## Context

A repo can hold [entire-records](https://github.com/entirehq/entire-records)
stores: schema-described structured data kept as git trees on
`refs/meta/records/<schema>/main`. Until now this service served only the raw
`(target, key, value)` triples, on `GET /repos/{id}/meta/targets`, leaving every
consumer to decode them.

Decoding is not a formatting step. The rules are not recoverable by looking at the
data: a record's shard is a hash of its id rather than an id prefix, a field's
`:type` and `:value` keys recombine into one value, keys no type declares are
dropped, an absent set encodes as `[]` where an absent scalar encodes as `null`,
and an ordered type's records are sorted by a rank field. A second implementation
gets most of that right and produces plausible-looking wrong records — which is
worse than failing.

entire-records' ADR `20260803-records-become-a-cell-api-concept` decided the
answer jointly with us: records become a concept of this service, and that repo
supplies the decode as a library above a two-method read seam (`store.Reader`).
entire.io's TypeScript app then fetches decoded records over one hop and contains
no records logic, which is what "no Go in that app" was asking for.

## Decision

**`internal/records` implements those two methods over this cell's git data plane,
and imports everything above them.** It is the third implementation of the seam —
a clone on disk and an HTTP client are the other two — and it adds no decode of
its own. The response bodies embed entire-records' own DTOs rather than mirroring
them, so the wire shape cannot drift from the decode that produces it. Nothing
guards the *field set* against an upstream rename, though: the spec test pins the
component names this service publishes, not their contents. That is a knowing gap
while the surface is on v0 — see the consequences below.

The dependency is pinned by pseudo-version on `main`. That repo has no tags and
deliberately deferred extracting a tagged decode module, so this is what
`entire-plans` already does. Go pins the commit, so an upstream change can only
break the build of whoever bumps it.

Three deliberate noes:

**Read-only.** Writes need an atomic multi-record commit. The single-key writes
git-meta offers today would leave a record observably half-written, which is worse
than offering none.

**No authorship, and no discards.** Both are derived by walking commit history.
A schema that wants provenance declares stamped fields (`stamp: writeTime` /
`writer`) and the answer arrives in the record's own fields at no cost, which is
what the reference UI already does. This keeps a read O(store) rather than
O(history) — and it leaves the wire shape untouched, so serving attribution later
(from a push-fed table rather than a per-request walk) is purely additive against
fields the contract already declares.

**Lists paginate, and the array is named `items`.** The several-types-at-one-commit
read returns a flat list rather than a map keyed by type: every record names its
own type, so grouping is the client's to do, and a page of a map of arrays has no
well-defined boundary. The page token carries the pinned commit and the scope, so
a continuation reads the tree its first page answered from. Paging bounds the
response, not the upstream read — the store has no partial read, so a page still
materialises the types it spans.

**The imported types are published under this service's names.** Response bodies
embed entire-records' DTOs, but a custom huma schema namer renames the whole
graph (`RecordDTO` → `RecordsRecord`). Declaring local mirrors would have been a
second statement of the wire shape — the thing most likely to drift — and a Go
type alias would not work at all, since an alias is the same type and reflection
still reports the original name. The gateway merges every cell service's spec into
one document and renames collisions to `<upstream>__<name>`, so publishing a name
as generic as `SchemaDTO` would let an unrelated service rename our clients' types.

**Unsettled is a version, not a path segment.** The routes are served on the v0
surface (`/api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/records…`): a Huma API and OpenAPI document of
their own, beside v1 rather than inside it, which the gateway serves at its v1
base with the version swapped. A path segment saying "experimental" would have to
change when the surface settles, and `api-review`'s VER-005 forbids it; VER-005
allows "a real version", and v0 is one. Routes leave v0 by moving to v1 under the
v1 rules, not by changing shape in place.

*Amended 2026-10-01.* This originally said the caveat lived in an OpenAPI tag on
the v1 document. A tag does not stop a client generating against the v1 document
and binding to shapes that are still moving, and v1 only allows additive changes
(VER-003). So the routes moved to v0 and left v1 without a deprecation window;
`entire-plans`' published-plans worker was the only known caller.

## Consequences

- **This service is now a consumer of another repo's Go API**, and one with no
  semver signal. What guards the seam is a set of unit tests over hand-built
  stores: the two-method reader (warming, the segment-aligned covering filter,
  failures not memoised as empty), the state conversion in both directions, and
  the read scoping. What is NOT guarded is an upstream field rename reaching this
  service's published spec — the check that would catch it is a byte-for-byte
  comparison against a store decoded by a reader we already trust.
- **That comparison was built and then removed, deliberately.** It existed
  because entire-api and entire-records held two independently-written
  implementations of the git-meta exchange format, meeting in one conversion
  function; a real store captured both ways was the cheapest proof they agreed.
  Those implementations are being merged, which removes the reason — and the
  fixture cost 238 KB of another repo's live data to carry. For an experimental,
  read-only surface that is the wrong trade. If this surface graduates before the
  merge lands, the check to restore is a small generated store (not a captured
  one), which would also cover the reference, nested and list-field shapes no
  capture of the planning store ever did.
- **A records read is more permissive about schema names than the raw git-meta
  read**, which rejects the uppercase in a camelCase schema name. entire-records'
  own name rule decides here, and it forbids dots and slashes, which is the
  property the namespace rule exists to enforce.
- **`?ref` is read as given**, so a pin taken from another store returns that
  store's records decoded against that store's schema: the path says where a read
  started, not what the pin contains. It cannot cross a repo — the pin must name a
  commit in this one — and it is the same latitude `/meta/targets` already allows.

## Amendment, 2026-10-10: reads come from strata

entire-plans made strata the authority for its records and kept git-meta only as
a mirror, and entire-api grew a strata write path. Serving reads from the mirror
would answer from a copy that lags the store and, for anything written through
entire-api, never receives it. So the records routes now read strata stores.

**The seam moved, the rule did not.** entire-records still does every decode;
what this service supplies is now a `store.Projection` — this cell's Postgres
projection of the store (`internal/recordprojection`), read through
`store.NewProjectionReader` — instead of a git-meta `store.Reader`. The git-meta
snapshot reader and its warming are gone.

**Every read catches up first, and nothing else does.** A read fetches the store
over git as the caller, into memory, and ticks the projection from its cursor
under a per-store advisory lock before answering. A write that has landed is
therefore visible to the next read without a pin, and a store nobody has
projected yet is bootstrapped by its first read.

**Over git, not the repo API.** A strata log entry carries its payload in its
commit message, and the repo API caps a message at 64 KiB in its JSON pages, so a
store with one large entry could never be read through it. git has no such cap,
and it is the transport the write path uses already. The background consumer
that followed ref events went with the repo API reader: it read cert-only, and
entiredb admits entire-api cert-only on the repo API but not for git fetches. A
read pays the catch-up for writes since the last read; if that shows up in
latency, the consumer can return once entiredb admits entire-api's git reads.

**`tip` names a state, not a commit.** A projection has no commit and no history.
`tip` is a hash of its cursor: equal for equal states, which is what a page token
needs to refuse a continuation after the store moved (409; the caller restarts).

**`?ref` is gone.** There is no history to pin to, and every read is already of
the current state, which is what read-your-writes needed it for. A caller that
still sends one is ignored rather than refused.

**Listing** names the repo's strata stores from `refs/strata/` and reports those
whose projection holds a schema.

The bullets above about `?ref` and the git-meta reader describe the surface as it
was until this amendment.
# A write socket is a strata writer's presence

Status: accepted, 2026-10-12.

## Decision

An editor holds a durable strata writer through one WebSocket,
`GET /api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/strata/{store}/sockets`. The writer is created when
the socket opens and evicted when it closes, so the connection is the writer's
presence. Edits arrive on it as records operations and are acknowledged on it;
what other writers do after the editor's read (`?changes_token=`) leaves on it as patches
and records, read the way the records changes stream reads them (ADR 0009),
without the records only this writer touched.

One-shot writes (`POST …/edits`) stay plain HTTP: each is its own writer,
announced, written and evicted in one ref transaction, with no presence to hold.

## Why a WebSocket, not SSE

This is a documented exception to PUBLIC-STREAM-001, which asks for server push
over SSE. The socket is not a push channel with writes beside it; it is one
session, and splitting it into an SSE stream plus POSTs would lose what the
session is for:

- **Presence needs one connection.** A strata writer holds back compaction until
  it is evicted, so its lifetime has to end when the editor leaves. With SSE plus
  POSTs, no single connection's end says the editor left: a POST can arrive after
  the stream dropped, on another replica, for a writer nobody holds any more.
- **One writer, one owner.** The writer's store is single-threaded, and the socket
  is the goroutine that owns it. POSTs would arrive on any replica and need the
  writer handed between them.
- **Ordering.** Frames on one socket are applied in order and acknowledged by
  sequence number. Independent POSTs would need ordering rebuilt on top.

On reconnect a client opens a new socket, as a new writer, and passes as `changes_token`
the token of the state it last holds; that is the outbound half's resume. The
rule does not require one on an ephemeral stream, but a token makes it free.

## Presence and cleanup

- **Lease.** A writer's lease row is taken before it announces itself and renewed
  while the socket is open. A writer whose renewal lapses fences itself, refuses
  further edits and closes the socket.
- **Crash backstop.** A replica that dies leaves its writers' leases to lapse. The
  next session on the store evicts lapsed writers, folds and retires them; there
  is no background sweeper.
- **Failed starts keep the lease.** Once the lease is taken the writer may already
  be announced, and only a leased writer can be evicted later.

## Authority

- Opening a socket and writing need `push` on the repo; creating a store needs
  `manage_settings`.
- Every git operation, maintenance included, runs on the caller's bearer. So any
  pusher can evict any lapsed writer; there is no entiredb carve-out.
- The bearer is re-checked every minute, and the socket ends before it expires,
  because ending the writer needs it.

## Placement

Strata writes are git pushes, which may enter at any placement that holds the
repo (PUBLIC-CELL-003's exception). Both the socket and the one-shot routes admit
on every cell, not only the processing primary.

## Consequences

- A client keeps each edit until a read shows it, and sends it again after
  reconnecting, so edits must be safe to repeat. The published app's are: an
  edit that already landed is a no-op.
- Any pusher can end another person's lapsed writer. That is the price of having
  no service-side authority over strata refs.
# A records read continues as a stream of changes

Status: accepted, 2026-10-12.

## Context

A records client that follows a store live has had one tool: watch the ref-event
stream for the store's refs and read the collections again whole whenever one
moves. The published planning app does exactly that, and while someone types it
re-reads the whole store about once a commit, in every open tab. The store is
small, so each read is cheap, but the rate is the commit rate times the number
of viewers, and every read ships every record to tell the reader about one.

The write socket already reports changes (ADR 0008), but only to an editor: a
socket is a writer, so it needs `push`, holds a lease and counts against the
replica's cap, and it leaves out its own writer's edits. A viewer has none of
those to spend and needs every writer's edits.

## Decision

**`GET /api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/records/{schema}/changes` streams what a store does
after a state the caller has read.** Server-sent events, gated like every
records read (`pull`).

- A collections read returns `changesToken` with its records. The stream starts
  from it (`?changes_token=`): not `since`, which this API's other operations
  use for RFC 3339 time bounds, and snake_case as RFD-026 asks of new
  parameters (the older records routes' camelCase is grandfathered).
- Each time the store's refs move, the stream reads what changed since the last
  state it reported and sends a `changed` event: what changed in records the
  caller holds, the records it cannot hold yet, and the ones that are gone. Its
  `id` is a token for the state they were read at,
  so an EventSource that reconnects resumes from `Last-Event-ID`, which is
  PUBLIC-STREAM-001's resume with the state as the thing resumed.
- `ready` marks the stream live. It ends with `reconnect` after a bounded time,
  and `forbidden` when access goes, like the other streams.

**What changed is read from the projection, not taken from the event.** The
ref-event hub is only the doorbell, as it is for the write socket. Every answer
catches the projection up first, like every records read, so a ring that lands
mid-read is answered by the next one and nothing falls between two.

**A record the caller holds comes back as a patch, decided and decoded here.**
The changed rows already say which fields moved, and a list's entries are rows of
their own, so a patch carries each changed field's value as the collections read
shapes it, or, for a list that only grew at its end, just the new entries and the
length the list now has. One keystroke into a body is one entry. Which changed
fields are entries pushed at a list's end is entire-records' to say
(`Snapshot.GetRecordChange`), from the same read that fetches the record and by
entry rather than by value, so no layout is taken apart here. Label, parent and
rank are restated whole. Anything an append cannot say, such as a fold removing
entries, sends that field whole. A record is held when one of its visible fields
predates the token and its delete floor has not risen since; anything else comes
back whole.

Not strata's ops. An op is undecided (many lose), and deciding it is
`record.Supersedes` plus delete floors, expiry and erasure; reading it as a
record is entire-records' decode. A browser doing both would be a third
implementation of the rules the projection's conformance cases and ADR 0005 exist
to keep in one place, and it would need every field's stamp, which no read
returns. The rows are the ops after they were decided, so a patch is about the
size of the op that caused it.

**A projection numbers its ticks, and each row records the tick that last wrote
it.** "What changed since a state" is then the rows whose tick is past the
state's. Ticks of one store are serialised by its advisory lock, so the numbers
commit in order. A tick that writes no row takes no number.

The per-writer cursor would also answer the question, exactly, but it grows with
every writer that has ever written to the store (one per editing session), and a
token carrying it would outgrow the header it has to travel in. A tick number
does not grow.

**The token is small and opaque:** generation, tick, schema version, and a digest
of the store's expiry and erasure sets. A row is only rewritten when its value is
superseded, so an unchanged tick means nothing a reader holds has moved.

**When a change cannot be told as records, the stream says `reload` and ends.**
That covers a new generation, a schema version the token did not read, a
projection behind the token, and an expiry or erasure (they delete rows rather
than write them, so no tick names what they took). The client reads the
collections again and opens a new stream from that read's token. A reload carries
no `id`, so an EventSource that reconnects anyway resumes from the last good
token and is told again.

**The write socket tells its editor the same way.** It takes the changesToken
of the read the editor's page made (`?changes_token=`, refused when this service did not
issue it) and, at once and then on each ring, reads what changed since with this
stream's read, less the records only its own writer touched: each projection row
names the writer that decided it. A ring that moved only its own writer's log is
its own write coming back, and is not read. Editors get patches too, and one set
of reload rules covers both. The writer's own feed cursor, which the socket used
to answer from, is gone. A socket opened without `changes_token` reports no changes.

## Consequences

# Records are read through entire-records' own decode

Status: accepted, 2026-08-10; amended 2026-10-01 (records move to the v0 surface); amended 2026-10-10 (reads come from strata)

## Context

A repo can hold [entire-records](https://github.com/entirehq/entire-records)
stores: schema-described structured data kept as git trees on
`refs/meta/records/<schema>/main`. Until now this service served only the raw
`(target, key, value)` triples, on `GET /repos/{id}/meta/targets`, leaving every
consumer to decode them.

Decoding is not a formatting step. The rules are not recoverable by looking at the
data: a record's shard is a hash of its id rather than an id prefix, a field's
`:type` and `:value` keys recombine into one value, keys no type declares are
dropped, an absent set encodes as `[]` where an absent scalar encodes as `null`,
and an ordered type's records are sorted by a rank field. A second implementation
gets most of that right and produces plausible-looking wrong records — which is
worse than failing.

entire-records' ADR `20260803-records-become-a-cell-api-concept` decided the
answer jointly with us: records become a concept of this service, and that repo
supplies the decode as a library above a two-method read seam (`store.Reader`).
entire.io's TypeScript app then fetches decoded records over one hop and contains
no records logic, which is what "no Go in that app" was asking for.

## Decision

**`internal/records` implements those two methods over this cell's git data plane,
and imports everything above them.** It is the third implementation of the seam —
a clone on disk and an HTTP client are the other two — and it adds no decode of
its own. The response bodies embed entire-records' own DTOs rather than mirroring
them, so the wire shape cannot drift from the decode that produces it. Nothing
guards the *field set* against an upstream rename, though: the spec test pins the
component names this service publishes, not their contents. That is a knowing gap
while the surface is on v0 — see the consequences below.

The dependency is pinned by pseudo-version on `main`. That repo has no tags and
deliberately deferred extracting a tagged decode module, so this is what
`entire-plans` already does. Go pins the commit, so an upstream change can only
break the build of whoever bumps it.

Three deliberate noes:

**Read-only.** Writes need an atomic multi-record commit. The single-key writes
git-meta offers today would leave a record observably half-written, which is worse
than offering none.

**No authorship, and no discards.** Both are derived by walking commit history.
A schema that wants provenance declares stamped fields (`stamp: writeTime` /
`writer`) and the answer arrives in the record's own fields at no cost, which is
what the reference UI already does. This keeps a read O(store) rather than
O(history) — and it leaves the wire shape untouched, so serving attribution later
(from a push-fed table rather than a per-request walk) is purely additive against
fields the contract already declares.

**Lists paginate, and the array is named `items`.** The several-types-at-one-commit
read returns a flat list rather than a map keyed by type: every record names its
own type, so grouping is the client's to do, and a page of a map of arrays has no
well-defined boundary. The page token carries the pinned commit and the scope, so
a continuation reads the tree its first page answered from. Paging bounds the
response, not the upstream read — the store has no partial read, so a page still
materialises the types it spans.

**The imported types are published under this service's names.** Response bodies
embed entire-records' DTOs, but a custom huma schema namer renames the whole
graph (`RecordDTO` → `RecordsRecord`). Declaring local mirrors would have been a
second statement of the wire shape — the thing most likely to drift — and a Go
type alias would not work at all, since an alias is the same type and reflection
still reports the original name. The gateway merges every cell service's spec into
one document and renames collisions to `<upstream>__<name>`, so publishing a name
as generic as `SchemaDTO` would let an unrelated service rename our clients' types.

**Unsettled is a version, not a path segment.** The routes are served on the v0
surface (`/api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/records…`): a Huma API and OpenAPI document of
their own, beside v1 rather than inside it, which the gateway serves at its v1
base with the version swapped. A path segment saying "experimental" would have to
change when the surface settles, and `api-review`'s VER-005 forbids it; VER-005
allows "a real version", and v0 is one. Routes leave v0 by moving to v1 under the
v1 rules, not by changing shape in place.

*Amended 2026-10-01.* This originally said the caveat lived in an OpenAPI tag on
the v1 document. A tag does not stop a client generating against the v1 document
and binding to shapes that are still moving, and v1 only allows additive changes
(VER-003). So the routes moved to v0 and left v1 without a deprecation window;
`entire-plans`' published-plans worker was the only known caller.

## Consequences

- **This service is now a consumer of another repo's Go API**, and one with no
  semver signal. What guards the seam is a set of unit tests over hand-built
  stores: the two-method reader (warming, the segment-aligned covering filter,
  failures not memoised as empty), the state conversion in both directions, and
  the read scoping. What is NOT guarded is an upstream field rename reaching this
  service's published spec — the check that would catch it is a byte-for-byte
  comparison against a store decoded by a reader we already trust.
- **That comparison was built and then removed, deliberately.** It existed
  because entire-api and entire-records held two independently-written
  implementations of the git-meta exchange format, meeting in one conversion
  function; a real store captured both ways was the cheapest proof they agreed.
  Those implementations are being merged, which removes the reason — and the
  fixture cost 238 KB of another repo's live data to carry. For an experimental,
  read-only surface that is the wrong trade. If this surface graduates before the
  merge lands, the check to restore is a small generated store (not a captured
  one), which would also cover the reference, nested and list-field shapes no
  capture of the planning store ever did.
- **A records read is more permissive about schema names than the raw git-meta
  read**, which rejects the uppercase in a camelCase schema name. entire-records'
  own name rule decides here, and it forbids dots and slashes, which is the
  property the namespace rule exists to enforce.
- **`?ref` is read as given**, so a pin taken from another store returns that
  store's records decoded against that store's schema: the path says where a read
  started, not what the pin contains. It cannot cross a repo — the pin must name a
  commit in this one — and it is the same latitude `/meta/targets` already allows.

## Amendment, 2026-10-10: reads come from strata

entire-plans made strata the authority for its records and kept git-meta only as
a mirror, and entire-api grew a strata write path. Serving reads from the mirror
would answer from a copy that lags the store and, for anything written through
entire-api, never receives it. So the records routes now read strata stores.

**The seam moved, the rule did not.** entire-records still does every decode;
what this service supplies is now a `store.Projection` — this cell's Postgres
projection of the store (`internal/recordprojection`), read through
`store.NewProjectionReader` — instead of a git-meta `store.Reader`. The git-meta
snapshot reader and its warming are gone.

**Every read catches up first, and nothing else does.** A read fetches the store
over git as the caller, into memory, and ticks the projection from its cursor
under a per-store advisory lock before answering. A write that has landed is
therefore visible to the next read without a pin, and a store nobody has
projected yet is bootstrapped by its first read.

**Over git, not the repo API.** A strata log entry carries its payload in its
commit message, and the repo API caps a message at 64 KiB in its JSON pages, so a
store with one large entry could never be read through it. git has no such cap,
and it is the transport the write path uses already. The background consumer
that followed ref events went with the repo API reader: it read cert-only, and
entiredb admits entire-api cert-only on the repo API but not for git fetches. A
read pays the catch-up for writes since the last read; if that shows up in
latency, the consumer can return once entiredb admits entire-api's git reads.

**`tip` names a state, not a commit.** A projection has no commit and no history.
`tip` is a hash of its cursor: equal for equal states, which is what a page token
needs to refuse a continuation after the store moved (409; the caller restarts).

**`?ref` is gone.** There is no history to pin to, and every read is already of
the current state, which is what read-your-writes needed it for. A caller that
still sends one is ignored rather than refused.

**Listing** names the repo's strata stores from `refs/strata/` and reports those
whose projection holds a schema.

The bullets above about `?ref` and the git-meta reader describe the surface as it
was until this amendment.
# A write socket is a strata writer's presence

Status: accepted, 2026-10-12.

## Decision

An editor holds a durable strata writer through one WebSocket,
`GET /api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/strata/{store}/sockets`. The writer is created when
the socket opens and evicted when it closes, so the connection is the writer's
presence. Edits arrive on it as records operations and are acknowledged on it;
what other writers do after the editor's read (`?changes_token=`) leaves on it as patches
and records, read the way the records changes stream reads them (ADR 0009),
without the records only this writer touched.

One-shot writes (`POST …/edits`) stay plain HTTP: each is its own writer,
announced, written and evicted in one ref transaction, with no presence to hold.

## Why a WebSocket, not SSE

This is a documented exception to PUBLIC-STREAM-001, which asks for server push
over SSE. The socket is not a push channel with writes beside it; it is one
session, and splitting it into an SSE stream plus POSTs would lose what the
session is for:

- **Presence needs one connection.** A strata writer holds back compaction until
  it is evicted, so its lifetime has to end when the editor leaves. With SSE plus
  POSTs, no single connection's end says the editor left: a POST can arrive after
  the stream dropped, on another replica, for a writer nobody holds any more.
- **One writer, one owner.** The writer's store is single-threaded, and the socket
  is the goroutine that owns it. POSTs would arrive on any replica and need the
  writer handed between them.
- **Ordering.** Frames on one socket are applied in order and acknowledged by
  sequence number. Independent POSTs would need ordering rebuilt on top.

On reconnect a client opens a new socket, as a new writer, and passes as `changes_token`
the token of the state it last holds; that is the outbound half's resume. The
rule does not require one on an ephemeral stream, but a token makes it free.

## Presence and cleanup

- **Lease.** A writer's lease row is taken before it announces itself and renewed
  while the socket is open. A writer whose renewal lapses fences itself, refuses
  further edits and closes the socket.
- **Crash backstop.** A replica that dies leaves its writers' leases to lapse. The
  next session on the store evicts lapsed writers, folds and retires them; there
  is no background sweeper.
- **Failed starts keep the lease.** Once the lease is taken the writer may already
  be announced, and only a leased writer can be evicted later.

## Authority

- Opening a socket and writing need `push` on the repo; creating a store needs
  `manage_settings`.
- Every git operation, maintenance included, runs on the caller's bearer. So any
  pusher can evict any lapsed writer; there is no entiredb carve-out.
- The bearer is re-checked every minute, and the socket ends before it expires,
  because ending the writer needs it.

## Placement

Strata writes are git pushes, which may enter at any placement that holds the
repo (PUBLIC-CELL-003's exception). Both the socket and the one-shot routes admit
on every cell, not only the processing primary.

## Consequences

- A client keeps each edit until a read shows it, and sends it again after
  reconnecting, so edits must be safe to repeat. The published app's are: an
  edit that already landed is a no-op.
- Any pusher can end another person's lapsed writer. That is the price of having
  no service-side authority over strata refs.
# A records read continues as a stream of changes

Status: accepted, 2026-10-12.

## Context

A records client that follows a store live has had one tool: watch the ref-event
stream for the store's refs and read the collections again whole whenever one
moves. The published planning app does exactly that, and while someone types it
re-reads the whole store about once a commit, in every open tab. The store is
small, so each read is cheap, but the rate is the commit rate times the number
of viewers, and every read ships every record to tell the reader about one.

The write socket already reports changes (ADR 0008), but only to an editor: a
socket is a writer, so it needs `push`, holds a lease and counts against the
replica's cap, and it leaves out its own writer's edits. A viewer has none of
those to spend and needs every writer's edits.

## Decision

**`GET /api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/records/{schema}/changes` streams what a store does
after a state the caller has read.** Server-sent events, gated like every
records read (`pull`).

- A collections read returns `changesToken` with its records. The stream starts
  from it (`?changes_token=`): not `since`, which this API's other operations
  use for RFC 3339 time bounds, and snake_case as RFD-026 asks of new
  parameters (the older records routes' camelCase is grandfathered).
- Each time the store's refs move, the stream reads what changed since the last
  state it reported and sends a `changed` event: what changed in records the
  caller holds, the records it cannot hold yet, and the ones that are gone. Its
  `id` is a token for the state they were read at,
  so an EventSource that reconnects resumes from `Last-Event-ID`, which is
  PUBLIC-STREAM-001's resume with the state as the thing resumed.
- `ready` marks the stream live. It ends with `reconnect` after a bounded time,
  and `forbidden` when access goes, like the other streams.

**What changed is read from the projection, not taken from the event.** The

catches the projection up first, like every records read, so a ring that lands
mid-read is answered by the next one and nothing falls between two.

**A record the caller holds comes back as a patch, decided and decoded here.**
The changed rows already say which fields moved, and a list's entries are rows of
their own, so a patch carries each changed field's value as the collections read
shapes it, or, for a list that only grew at its end, just the new entries and the
length the list now has. One keystroke into a body is one entry. Which changed
fields are entries pushed at a list's end is entire-records' to say

rank are restated whole. Anything an append cannot say, such as a fold removing
entries, sends that field whole. A record is held when one of its visible fields
predates the token and its delete floor has not risen since; anything else comes
back whole.

Not strata's ops. An op is undecided (many lose), and deciding it is
`record.Supersedes` plus delete floors, expiry and erasure; reading it as a
record is entire-records' decode. A browser doing both would be a third
implementation of the rules the projection's conformance cases and ADR 0005 exist
to keep in one place, and it would need every field's stamp, which no read
returns. The rows are the ops after they were decided, so a patch is about the
size of the op that caused it.

**A projection numbers its ticks, and each row records the tick that last wrote

state's. Ticks of one store are serialised by its advisory lock, so the numbers
commit in order. A tick that writes no row takes no number.

every writer that has ever written to the store (one per editing session), and a
token carrying it would outgrow the header it has to travel in. A tick number
does not grow.

**The token is small and opaque:** generation, tick, schema version, and a digest
of the store's expiry and erasure sets. A row is only rewritten when its value is
superseded, so an unchanged tick means nothing a reader holds has moved.

**When a change cannot be told as records, the stream says `reload` and ends.**
That covers a new generation, a schema version the token did not read, a
projection behind the token, and an expiry or erasure (they delete rows rather
than write them, so no tick names what they took). The client reads the
collections again and opens a new stream from that read's token. A reload carries
no `id`, so an EventSource that reconnects anyway resumes from the last good
token and is told again.

**The write socket tells its editor the same way.** It takes the changesToken
of the read the editor's page made (`?changes_token=`, refused when this service did not
issue it) and, at once and then on each ring, reads what changed since with this
stream's read, less the records only its own writer touched: each projection row
names the writer that decided it. A ring that moved only its own writer's log is
its own write coming back, and is not read. Editors get patches too, and one set
of reload rules covers both. The writer's own feed cursor, which the socket used
to answer from, is gone. A socket opened without `changes_token` reports no changes.

## Consequences

- A viewer following a store pays one small event per commit instead of a whole
  read, and an editor's edits reach the viewer the same way as anyone else's.

# A follower may read on without the history behind it

A Follower that is handed a **Since** — the commit each of the store's
generations and each writer's newest log named when it last read, and the
erasures in force then — reads only the entries written after it, and needs no
other object. `FetchFor` says what to fetch for
that read; `Follower.FeedSince` reads it and returns the next Since.

## Context

`Feed` is O(tail): it walks every live log from its tip to the root of its
rotation, reads the newest generation's description, and restates the erasure set
from both on every batch. On a clone that keeps its repository that is a cost in
CPU. On a reader that keeps nothing between reads — entire-api's records
projection opens an empty in-memory repository per tick and has its read model
in Postgres — it is a cost in transfer: every tick that anything moved fetches
the whole tail and the newest generation's tree to apply a handful of ops.

What such a reader can keep is small: the tips it read, which git's fetch
negotiation turns into "send me what is newer than these", and the erasure set,
which is the one thing a batch restates that cannot be read from new entries.

## Decision

**A Since records what a feed reads, and nothing else.** The generations, and
each writer's newest log. Announcements and evictions a feed reads only by name,
and an older rotation is one a prune is still withdrawing; `Tips` leaves them
out, and every party that compares a listing against a Since uses it.

**A read goes on from a Since only across changes that add entries.** A log
growing or a writer's first log appearing. A generation published, a log
rotated, or a log or generation deleted by retirement or retention makes the
read whole. Those are exactly the changes that discharge erasures,
reseed a projection or drop entries, so between two incremental reads the
erasure set only grows by what the new entries carry, and carrying it forward is
exact rather than an approximation.

**One function decides, for the fetch and for the read.** `FetchFor` applies it to
what the remote advertises, `FeedSince` to the refs it was handed. A fetch that
planned an incremental read and a read that went whole — or the reverse — is the
failure this rules out.

**It is Feed, over a survey told where to stop.** Reading on differs from a whole
read in two answers only: the tail is read back to the Since's tips, and the
erasures in force start from its set rather than the newest generation's. The
survey takes the Since and gives those two answers; the batch is assembled by
the same code either way.

**Logs are walked by parent, not by Log.** `Reader.Log(tip)` returns everything
reachable, and the commits before the stopping point are not held. `git.Commit`
now carries its parents, and the incremental read walks first parents with
`Commit` until it reaches the commit the Since names. On the git binary that is
a process per new entry, which is the size of the tick. A log that does not reach
back to it is `ErrNotIncremental`, never an answer from the entries it does
hold; the caller reads whole.

**An unchanged generation is not read.** Its erasures are already in the Since,
and nothing else in a feed at a caught-up cursor needs it.

**The Since sits beside the cursor, not inside it.** `project.Cursor` is how far a
read model has consumed and means the same over any transport. A Since is where
in a repository that consumption was read from.

## Consequences

- A reader that keeps nothing fetches, per tick, the new entries and nothing
  else, and fetches whole around compaction and prune: never more than it did
  before.
- The reader keeps the Since durably with its cursor and in the same
  transaction, so the two cannot describe different reads.
- Every driver fills `Commit.Parents`. The conformance suite checks it against
  `Log`.
- `Feed` is unchanged and remains O(tail) for a clone that holds everything.
# A store has one remote

A store's remote is the remote whose fetch refspecs fetch the store. Once one
does, `Configure` refuses any other name with `ErrSecondRemote`. The same name
may still be pointed at a new URL. Other remotes in the repository, such as the
code's own `origin` or `upstream`, are not the store's business and are not
counted.

## Context

The API never said how many remotes a store could have. `Configure`, `Push`,
`Fetch` and `Sync` all take a remote by name, tracking refs are laid out per
remote, and capabilities are cached per remote. Nothing tested more than one,
and the CLI configures only `origin`.

Reviewing ADR-0026 found that a store with two remotes is unsafe in three ways,
and two of them lose data silently:

- **Retention** measured from the newest generation across every remote. A push
  to the lagging remote could withdraw its newest generation while the
  generation replacing it existed only on the other remote. That generation is
  what the lagging remote's logs were pruned against.
- **Prune** has the same flaw, and it was on `main` before ADR-0026. It prunes a
  writer's log against the newest generation in the merged view. A push to a
  remote that lacks that generation then publishes the pruned log without it.
  Push never offers a generation this clone only holds as another remote's
  tracking ref, so nothing brings the missing generation across.
- **The push queue** is one per store. `Push(remote)` empties it, so a second
  remote never receives the refs the first push took.

All three have one cause: the survey reads `refs/strata-tracking/*` as a single
view, and the queue does not know about remotes.

## Decision

**One remote per store, refused at `Configure`.** That makes all three hazards
unreachable through the API, and it costs nothing today: the only user has one
remote.

**Retention guards per destination anyway.** `withdrawGenerations` withdraws a
generation only from a remote whose listing holds a newer one (ADR-0026). It is
cheap. It is also the right check even with one remote, because a remote's
newest generation is the one thing retention must never take from it.

**The remote is read from its refspec, not recorded.** The first version
recorded the name under `strata.<store>.remote`. `git remote rename` left that
naming a remote that no longer existed, and `Configure` then refused the new
name for ever. Git carries a remote's refspecs through a rename, so reading
them back cannot go stale. It also finds the remote for a clone configured
before anything was recorded. Two remotes that both fetch the store can only
come from configuration written by hand; they are refused, not chosen between.

Announcing uses the same answer. It used to take the first remote `git remote`
listed, which is sorted, so a code remote named `github` beside `origin` was
fetched in place of the store's.

A rename leaves two things behind, and both are left alone. The tracking refs
stay under the old name, and the renamed remote's refspec still writes there
when plain `git fetch` runs. Neither can lose data: both are older copies of
the same remote, so neither holds a generation newer than the remote does.

There is no check in `Open` and no status line. No store has two remotes yet,
so there is nothing to detect, and refusing in `Open` could lock someone out of
reading their own data.

## Lifting it

Several remotes need two things this design lacks:
- a survey taken for a destination, which reads that remote's tracking refs and
  the local ones and nothing else
- a push queue per remote

With both, Prune and Retain judge against what the destination holds, and every
remote receives every ref. `Announce`, `Push`, `Fetch` and `Sync` already take a
remote by name for that day. Until then, a second remote is a refusal.
# Push authorization is a server-side policy, not a log in the repository

Write access to a repository is push access to every store in it. Git has no
per-ref authorization, and nothing in this protocol changes that: a store's refs
are ordinary refs. So the boundary a group actually gets is whatever the server
enforces at receive time.

We enforce it with a `pre-receive` hook (`cmd/strata-receive`) over a policy that
lives on the server's disk, at `$GIT_DIR/strata-policy`. The decision itself is a
pure function — `authz.Check(policy, identity, updates)` — with no git in it, so
it is testable without a repository and the hook is a thin composition around it.

A grant is per writer, not per store:

```
allow alice refs/strata/alpha/log/W1/*
allow alice refs/strata/alpha/announced/W1
allow alice refs/strata/alpha/gen/*
```

`authz.Grant` generates those three lines, because the ref layout is the
protocol's business and a hand-written policy file is a second copy of it that
diverges silently. The mistake worth designing out is a single
`refs/strata/alpha/*` pattern: it hands every member every other member's log,
and it looks reasonable.

## Why not gittuf

gittuf is the better answer to the part we have not solved. It has key
distribution, rotation and revocation, and it keeps policy in the repository
rather than in a forge, which is the stance this project takes everywhere else.

It also records every reference update as an entry in one hash-chained log at
`refs/gittuf/reference-state-log`. Every writer appends to that one ref and each
entry names its predecessor, so concurrent appends cannot merge: a loser fetches,
rebuilds and retries. Measured here (`mise run gittuf-cost`):

| writers | appends | own refs refused | elapsed | attempts per append | gave up after 12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 20 | 0 | 4.3s | 2.5 | 0 |
| 8 | 40 | 0 | 13.4s | 4.5 | 0 |
| 16 | 80 | 0 | 43.1s | 7.4 | 9 |

Eight writers pushing only their own refs, for comparison: 0.41s, nothing
refused. This project exists
because a shared-ref design collapsed under exactly that contention. Adopting one
on the push path would undo its founding premise.

Policy *in the repository* is separable from the RSL in principle, but not for
free: it needs a trusted root to bootstrap from and a gated path for its own
updates, which is most of what makes gittuf gittuf. A policy file on the server's
disk needs neither, because it is not pushable. It is a smaller claim, and it is
one that can be kept.

## Consequences

**The identity comes from the environment and never from the push.** The hook
reads `STRATA_IDENTITY` (or the variable `STRATA_IDENTITY_VAR` names), which the
server's access layer sets — an SSH forced command's record of which key
authenticated, a proxy's authenticated user. Never a push option: those are sent
by the client as part of the push being authorized, so an identity taken from one
is a self-declaration. The same disqualifies the committer and author fields.

**A missing policy denies.** A repository nobody configured fails on its first
push rather than on its first incident.

**A grant per writer could not express ending one.** Evict and Retire act on
somebody else's refs, so the operational verbs this project ships could not be
used against a deployment running the hook at all. The store-wide pattern refused
above is now expressible with the dangerous verb withheld, which is
[ADR-0015](0015-an-operator-grant-withholds-a-verb-rather-than-narrowing-a-pattern.md).
The objection here stands: it is to what update permits, not to breadth.

**`Grant` generated the lines and still fell behind the layout, so the layout
moved.** Recorded here because this decision is where the reasoning was, and the
reasoning was half applied. Generating the three lines removed one copy of the ref
layout — the hand-written policy file — and left another: `authz` still named the
kinds of ref itself, in `Grant` and again in the shape check. The layout then
gained an eviction ref and `authz` did not hear about it, so `refs/strata/<store>/evicted/<writer>`
was refused as an unknown kind, which is the push that releases the barrier
(ADR-0002) — a one-shot writer could not close itself and compaction stopped. No
test caught it because catching it needs the store's half and the hook's half in
view at once, and no package held both. Both halves are now `reflayout`, which
`store` and `authz` read; the grant is four lines; and an import-boundary test
fails on any shipped code that spells a record ref out for itself.

**A published generation may be created or deleted, never replaced** — for
everyone, including an identity the policy trusts completely. Generations are
verified by recomputation, which works only while the bytes at a number stay the
bytes everyone folded. Replacing them leaves no evidence any later read could
find: a clone that already adopted the old generation simply holds different data
from one that adopts the new one, for ever. Creating and deleting are how
generations are meant to move — published once, dropped by retention.

**Refs the layout does not describe are refused** whatever the policy says. An
unrecognised shape under `refs/strata/` is a mistake or an attempt.

**A path remote authorizes nothing.** `git push /path/to/repo.git` runs
`receive-pack` as a child of the pushing process, so the environment the hook sees
is the pusher's. The hermetic tests here prove the hook — that the right refs are
refused, that a refusal takes the whole push down, that a missing policy denies —
and they prove nothing about authentication, which a path remote does not have.

**This is not signing.** A signature says who wrote a value, survives compaction,
and is checked by readers; it lives on the record and outside the protocol
(ADR-0008). This says who may move a ref, is checked once by the server, and
protects the parts of the layout no later reader could tell had been tampered
with. Neither substitutes for the other.
# A one-shot writer is authorised by shape, not by name

A one-shot writer's identity is 130 bits of `crypto/rand` minted as it commits,
and it must be: two processes that both claimed one identity would hand the same
sequence number to different ops, and `(writer, seq)` is what ops deduplicate by —
silent, permanent divergence. So the identity cannot be derived from a runner, a
machine or a job, and no `authz` grant can name it in advance.

The consequence was that CI reporting — the use case one-shot writers exist for
([ADR-0002](0002-a-one-shot-writer-evicts-itself.md)) — worked against a path
remote and against a server that authorises nothing, and not against one that
does.

## The rule

A grant that names a store rather than a writer:

```
allow-oneshot ci refs/strata/alpha
```

It permits creating `announced/<W>`, `log/<W>/0` and `evicted/<W>` — all three,
all as creations, for one `W`, with nothing else of that writer's in the push.
That sentence is the glossary's definition of a **one-shot writer** ("creates
its log, writes once, never appends, and evicts itself on completion") turned
into a predicate, which is why the rule word names the term rather than coining
one.

It is decidable from the update set alone. A `pre-receive` hook runs once per push
and is handed every ref it proposes, and `Check` already received them together —
so this stays a pure function with no git in it, like the rest of the package.

## Why the shape is enough

Everything that keeps the grant narrow falls out of the shape rather than needing
a check of its own:

- **It cannot be grafted onto a writer that already exists.** That writer's
  announcement is already on the server, so an update naming it is not a
  creation, and the set is short. This is what a create-only grant over `log/*`
  could not do: creating `log/<existing>/<n>` makes it that writer's log tip,
  because a read takes the highest rotation.
- **It cannot append later.** Rotation zero is named, and one ref arriving alone
  is not a whole writer.
- **It cannot introduce a writer that does not close itself.** The eviction is one
  of the three, so ADR-0002's contract stops being a convention the client is
  trusted to keep and becomes a condition of being let in. A writer admitted
  without one would count toward the barrier for ever, and there would be no clone
  left to evict it — the operator grant
  ([ADR-0015](0015-an-operator-grant-withholds-a-verb-rather-than-narrowing-a-pattern.md))
  can end a writer, but only one somebody knows about.

## Considered options

**Marking ephemeral writers in the ref layout**, so an ordinary prefix pattern
could cover them. Conceptually simplest and needs no new rule shape. Rejected on
cost and blast radius: eight sites in `reflayout` including `classify` and the
store-name probe, `view.absorb`, `currentRotation`, `Retire`'s enumeration, and
five pinning tests whose entire purpose is to make a change to ref *names* loud —
because two clones on different builds meet on a remote that holds both.

**A registration step**, where the runner asks the server for an identity first.
Closest to how such systems usually work and it would make revocation possible.
Rejected because it needs a service and a protocol where today there is a file on
disk, which is most of what ADR-0012 chose a static policy to avoid.

## Consequences

**An identity holding this grant can create writers freely.** That is the
capability, not a leak: a CI runner reports many runs and each is a writer. What
it cannot do is touch a writer it did not create in that same push.

**A one-shot writer now fetches before it announces.** It publishes a low-water
mark — a promise never to write below a Lamport value — and a promise made
against a view this clone has not refreshed promises something already false:
the ops land below a boundary already folded, belong to no generation, and the
next prune destroys them. [ADR-0009](0009-membership-must-be-announced.md) says
announcing is where connectivity is required; this path returned before
`mustBeAnnounced` and had no equivalent, so it never followed the rule that
already covered it. It mattered little while a one-shot could not push to a
guarded server at all. It matters now, and a CI runner is the likeliest clone in
this design never to have fetched.

**Writing is still offline for everyone else.** The fetch happens only where a
remote is configured, and only on the path that announces.
